>
> >

> > 3) How can I change the white grid in the background? In some cases I'd
> like to
> > remove the white grid
>
> A group of enterprising ggplot2 users recently put together a page of
> user-defined themes for the community:
> https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/themes/
>
> Another one, called 'theme_nothing' and authored by David Kahle of
> Rice U., blanks out most of the options in a ggplot:
>
> # david kahle
> # sept 27, 2010
>
> theme_nothing <- function (base_size = 12){
> structure(list(
> axis.line = theme_blank(),
> axis.text.x = theme_blank(),
> axis.text.y = theme_blank(),
> axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
> axis.title.x = theme_blank(),
> axis.title.y = theme_blank(),
> axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "lines"),
> axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
> legend.position = "none",
> panel.background = theme_blank(),
> panel.border = theme_blank(),
> panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
> panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
> panel.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
> plot.background = theme_blank(),
> plot.title = theme_text(size = base_size * 1.2),
> plot.margin = unit(c(-1, -1, -1.5, -1.5), "lines")),
> class = "options")
> }
>
> You could study these themes to get an idea how to create one of your
> own that retains the features you desire.

If you look at the scale_brewer help page and look carefully at the
palette item, you'll see a snippet of code that you can copy and paste
into your R session that will return the various ColorBrewer palettes
available in R. Note that the ColorBrewer palettes are for use with
discrete scales with a limited number of levels (max 7-9 depending on
the palette). Other color palettes can be made available through the
colorRamp() and colorRampPalette() functions from the grDevices
package (autoloaded), the colorspace package, the vcd package, the
munsell package and undoubtedly several other packages with similar
capabilities. Hadley's book shows an example where color palettes are
created from functions in the vcd package (which in turn uses the
colorspace package) and then transported to ggplot2. The code is
available on the book website in the chapter titled 'Scales, axes and
legends'. [http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/book/scales.r ] Look for a
commented paragraph that starts with 'Gradient color scales'; the code
beneath it shows how to write a function to create a palette that you
can pass into a ggplot call, with a couple of illustrative examples.

The point of this long-winded response is that the set of potential
palettes one can use is more or less up to you, because there are many
possibilities available. There are a few papers/talks available
on-line about the use of color in R, and the vast majority of it
should be transportable to ggplot2.

HTH,
Dennis
